Clearance

From the ramp to the flight levels
Tap an airport · drag to turn · pinch to zoom

The seats you don't work are run by the computer. Traffic comes in waves like a real hub: a lull, an arrival push, then a departure push.

Training

Short guided lessons, set at Phoenix. Start with Ground, then Tower, TRACON and Center. Each lesson you finish earns 50 XP. The coach tells you what to say and why.

Career

Progress is saved in this browser, so each device and site keeps its own career. Use a progress code below to move it.

Commands

Point and click

Click an aircraft (or its strip). Then build the clearance: drag from the aircraft to set a heading (drop it on a fix for a direct), click a fix for a direct, click a final approach course (dashed line off a runway) for the ILS, and pick altitude, speed and actions in the panel. The amber line shows what you're about to say. Press Transmit or Enter to read it to the cockpit; Esc scraps it.

Desired altitudes and speeds

Planning an arrival: 3 miles for every 1,000 ft to lose (11,000 ft over a 1,100 ft field needs about 30 miles). Slowing down eats distance too, so give the speed early: a jet can't descend steeply and slow down at the same time. Below 10,000 ft the limit is 250 kt. The altitudes below suit a field near 1,000 ft (Phoenix, Atlanta); at a sea-level field (LAX, John Wayne) work about 1,000 ft lower, or the jet arrives above the glideslope.

Landing tips

Turn them onto a heading that crosses the extended runway line at 30° or less, about 8 to 12 miles out, at 4,000 to 5,000 ft, then clear them for the ILS. They catch the glideslope from below and slow down on their own inside 5 miles.

Scoring

+10 each landing and each clean handoff. −10 lost separation, −10 leaving your airspace without a handoff, −5 terrain warning, −5 go-around because the runway was not clear, −3 approach too high.

On the scope: blue arrivals, green departures, yellow overflights (Center), purple incoming handoff, amber conflict ahead, red separation lost. Data block: callsign / altitude in hundreds with arrow and assigned altitude / ground speed and type (G350 = 350 kt over the ground).

Approach lanes (🛬 button on the scope, or Settings): a faint picture of the ideal arrival path for each landing runway, with downwind, base and final, and the altitude and speed to aim for on each leg. Off by default; turn it on as a crutch while you learn.

Center (ARTCC) seat: a high en-route sector, FL110 to FL410, 90 miles around the airport. Separation up here is 5 miles or 1,000 ft. Arrivals arrive at cruise: start them down with the 3-to-1 rule (3 miles per 1,000 ft to lose, plus a few to slow down) so they reach their arrival gate at the crossing altitude, then hand them to Approach within 40 miles of the gate and below FL240. Departures come up from Approach at about 17,000: climb them to their filed level and hand them to the next sector within 30 miles of the edge. Overflights (yellow) just cross; watch where their routes meet. Eastbound flights (course 000–179) fly odd levels such as FL350, westbound even levels such as FL360.

Parallel runways at least 3,600 ft apart (Atlanta, LAX, Phoenix) run side-by-side approaches: once two arrivals are established on different parallel localizers, they need no separation from each other. While they are still turning on, keep them 1,000 ft or 3 miles apart.

Two speeds: the speed you assign, shown as IAS in the side panel, is indicated airspeed, what the pilot flies. Ground speed (G on the scope, GS in the panel) is how fast it actually moves, and it reads well above IAS up high (280 IAS at 12,000 ft is about 350 over the ground). They come together near the runway.
